title: CLIP: Learning Visual Models from Language
hook: Skip the fixed label list. Train on image–caption pairs so pictures and text share one space, and you can classify images from plain-text labels you make up on the spot.
key_points: Trains on huge sets of image–caption pairs with a contrastive objective.
Puts images and text in a shared embedding space so they can be compared directly.
Classifies images zero-shot from arbitrary text labels, no task-specific training.
Its text–image alignment underpins text-to-image systems like later diffusion models.
content_html: Alec Radford, Jong Wook Kim, and colleagues at OpenAI trained CLIP on a huge collection of image–caption pairs scraped from the web, using a contrastive objective that pulls matching image and text embeddings together and pushes mismatched ones apart. The result is a shared space where you can compare a picture to any text. That lets CLIP classify images zero-shot from plain-language labels and gives generative models a way to align images with words.
extra_html:
How it works

CLIP has two encoders, one for images and one for text, trained together. For a batch of image–caption pairs, it computes embeddings for every image and every caption, then trains so each image is closest to its own caption and far from the others — a contrastive loss over all pairs in the batch. To classify a new image with no extra training, you embed candidate labels as short phrases like "a photo of a cat," embed the image, and pick the label whose text embedding is nearest.

Why it matters

Traditional image classifiers are locked to the categories they were trained on. CLIP breaks that by learning from natural language, so its vocabulary is open-ended and you can specify classes at test time just by typing them. Beyond classification, its joint image–text space became a key building block for text-to-image generation, where a text prompt needs to steer what an image should contain.

related.title: An Image is Worth 16x16 Words (ViT)
related.hook: Chop an image into patches, treat each like a word, and feed them to a plain Transformer. With enough pretraining data, it matches or beats convolutional networks.

related.title: High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion (Stable Diffusion)
related.hook: Running diffusion on raw pixels is brutally expensive. Do it in a compressed latent space instead, and high-res text-to-image becomes cheap enough to run on a consumer GPU.

related.title: DALL·E 2 (unCLIP): Text-to-Image with CLIP Latents
related.hook: Turn a prompt into a CLIP image embedding first, then diffusion-decode that embedding into a picture. A two-stage path from words to vivid, editable images.

prereqs.title: What Is Attention?
prereqs.hook: Attention lets a model decide what to focus on: it scores how relevant each piece of input is to the current question, then blends them by those scores.

flashcards.prompt: Why can CLIP classify images from labels you invent at test time?
flashcards.back_html: It learns a shared image-text embedding space, so you can embed any text label as a phrase and pick the one nearest the image — no task-specific training.

flashcards.prompt: Why are traditional image classifiers more limited than CLIP?
flashcards.back_html: They are locked to the fixed categories they were trained on, while CLIP learns from natural language, giving it an open-ended vocabulary set at test time.
